doc: Distance, walk-time and bearing rules. ADR-008's honesty applies to geography as much as to time: straight-line distance is an approximation, so metres are rounded to the nearest 10 and walk time to a whole minute, and nothing here pretends to be a road distance. Two conventions specific to this file: (1) the four float-returning groups compare with a `tolerance` in the same unit as the value, because no two languages' trigonometry libraries agree to the last bit — a port must assert |actual - expected| <= tolerance, NOT equality; (2) every rounding in this file is HALF-AWAY-FROM-ZERO on positives (JS `Math.round`, Swift `rounded()`, Kotlin `Math.round`). It is NOT banker's rounding: Kotlin's `Math.rint`, Python's `round()` and .NET's `Math.Round` default to half-to-even and will disagree on the .5 cases, which are called out individually below.

haversineMeters.doc: Great-circle distance between two WGS84 points, in metres, on a sphere of mean radius 6 371 008.8 m (the WGS84 authalic radius — a port must use the same constant or every figure drifts). Compare within `tolerance`.

cases.name: central-to-tsim-sha-tsui
cases.why: Across Victoria Harbour. About 2.35 km straight line; the real walk is a tunnel or a ferry, which is exactly why this is only ever shown as an approximation.

cases.name: identical-points-are-exactly-zero
cases.why: Tolerance 0: this must be exact, not near-zero. A port whose formula loses precision at zero would show a rider standing at the pole a non-zero distance.

cases.name: two-poles-of-one-place
cases.why: The scale that matters most: two kerbs of the same interchange, ~68 m apart. ADR-042 clustering lives at this scale, so a port that is accurate over kilometres but sloppy over tens of metres breaks place merging rather than distance labels.

cases.name: one-degree-of-latitude
cases.why: A scale-check independent of Hong Kong: one degree of latitude on this sphere. Equal to one degree of longitude at the equator, which catches a lat/lng transposition.

cases.name: antipodal-points-do-not-overflow
cases.why: Half the sphere's circumference. The formula clamps the argument of asin to 1, so floating-point error just past the antipode yields the maximum distance rather than NaN. A port that omits the clamp returns NaN here on some inputs and the distance column silently blanks.

routeDistanceM.doc: Total straight-line length of an ordered path — the sum of great-circle hops. Used as an APPROXIMATE bus-route distance from its stop coordinates, because HK open data carries no route polylines. It therefore UNDER-counts: a bus follows curving roads, not straight hops between stops. Only ever shown as an explicit estimate (ADR-008/ADR-044).

cases.name: single-point-is-zero
cases.why: One stop is not a journey. Guards the loop's first iteration, which has no predecessor.

cases.name: three-stops-sum-two-hops
cases.why: 2349.0794 + 2297.6258. Proves the hops are summed consecutively rather than measured origin-to-terminus, which would give a much shorter figure for any route that curves back.

cases.name: a-circular-route-returns-to-its-origin-with-a-non-zero-length
cases.why: The origin and terminus coincide, as on a circular route. Straight-line displacement is zero but the path length is not — the row that catches a port measuring first-to-last.

walkMinutes.doc: Estimated walking minutes for a straight-line distance at 80 m/min (~4.8 km/h), rounded to a whole minute with a floor of 1. The floor exists because '0 min walk' is not information.

cases.name: zero-distance-is-floored-to-one-minute
cases.why: Standing at the pole still reads '1 min walk'. Never 0.

cases.name: half-minute-rounds-up-to-one
cases.why: 40 m is exactly 0.5 min. Half-away-from-zero gives 1; the floor would give 1 anyway, so this row is only a partial discriminator — see the 200 m row for the real one.

cases.name: exact-half-minute-rounds-away-from-zero
cases.why: THE ROUNDING-MODE ROW. 200 m is exactly 2.5 min. Half-away-from-zero gives 3. Banker's rounding (Kotlin Math.rint, Python round, .NET default) gives 2 and this row goes red — which is the point.

formatDistance.doc: Human distance. Under 1 km: metres rounded to the nearest 10, no space before the unit ('200m'). At or above 1 km: one decimal ('1.2km'). Unit symbols are locale-neutral, so this takes no locale. The tight spacing is deliberate — this is a glanceable label, not prose.

cases.name: under-five-metres-reads-as-zero
cases.why: Rounding to the nearest 10 means 4 m shows '0m'. Acceptable: the rider is standing at the stop.

cases.name: five-metres-rounds-up-to-ten
cases.why: Half-away-from-zero on the tens.

cases.name: just-under-a-kilometre-prints-1000m
cases.why: FIXED 2026-07-28. The unit was chosen from the RAW distance, so 995-999 m took the metres path and then rounded to '1000m'. Rounding now happens first and the unit is chosen from the rounded value. Affected roughly one reading in 200, shown beside a neighbouring stop's '1.0km'.

cases.name: one-metre-under-a-kilometre-prints-1000m
cases.why: The far end of the same range. Two rows because 995-999 is what the fix had to cover, and a single row invites a port to special-case one value.

cases.name: exactly-one-kilometre-switches-unit
cases.why: The first value on the km branch. One decimal is mandatory, so '1.0km' not '1km'.

cases.name: km-exact-half-decimal-rounds-away-from-zero
cases.why: 1.25 km. Half-away-from-zero on the first decimal gives '1.3km'.

formatWalk.doc: Localized walk estimate for a single distance. The locale selects only the unit phrase; the figure is not localized. Note the English form has a space ('2 min walk') where formatDistance has none — the two labels sit next to each other and this asymmetry is intentional.

formatWalkRange.doc: Localized walk estimate across a RANGE of distances — the multi-pole place of ADR-042, where the poles of one place sit different walks away and quoting a single figure would be a guess about which kerb the rider wants. Collapses to one figure when the poles round to the same minute (never '4–4'), and is order-independent, so a caller may pass the two bounds either way round. The separator is U+2013 EN DASH with NO surrounding spaces — unlike formatHeadway, which spaces it. Both forms are deliberate and a port must not unify them.

cases.name: four-member-place-spans-two-walk-times
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (a 4-member place). Clustering has been N-member since ADR-042, so the interesting case is not a pair. A four-pole interchange with member walks of 320 m / 350 m / 410 m / 480 m reduces to 4 min and 6 min; the caller passes the extremes. A port that only ever handled two poles, or that averaged them, gets this wrong — and averaging would be the worse failure, because it invents a walk to a kerb that does not exist.

cases.name: four-member-place-order-independent
cases.why: The same four-pole place with the bounds swapped. Must produce the identical label, not '6–4'.

cases.name: four-member-place-collapses-when-every-pole-rounds-alike
cases.why: A four-pole place whose members are 310 m / 320 m / 330 m / 350 m — all 4 min. Never '4–4 min walk'.

cases.name: both-bounds-under-the-floor-collapse-to-one-minute
cases.why: Two poles 10 m and 30 m away both floor to 1 min, so no range appears.

formatBearing.doc: Localized 8-point compass direction for a MEAN TRAVEL BEARING, snapped to the nearest octant. This is the cue that tells two same-named places apart — the NE kerb from the SW kerb of one landmark (ADR-042) — so the label is '-bound' (a direction of travel), not a plain compass point. The input is degrees in ANY range: negatives and values over 360 are normalized first, which matters because a mean of bearings can legitimately come out negative. Octant index = round(normalized / 45) mod 8, over the table [N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW].

cases.name: snaps-down-just-below-the-midpoint
cases.why: 22 deg is nearer N than NE.

cases.name: exact-octant-midpoint-rounds-away-from-zero
cases.why: 22.5 deg is exactly between N and NE, i.e. round(0.5). Half-away-from-zero gives octant 1 (NE); half-to-even gives octant 0 (N). This row separates the two rounding modes.

cases.name: wraps-past-northwest-back-to-north
cases.why: 337.5 deg rounds to octant 8, which is taken modulo 8 back to North. A port that indexes an 8-element table without the modulo reads out of bounds here — a crash, or an empty label.

cases.name: negative-bearing-is-normalized
cases.why: -45 deg is 315 deg. A mean of bearings either side of north can come out negative, so this is reachable, not hypothetical. A port using a bare `%` on a negative gets a negative index.

cases.name: octant-1-northeast-zh-hant
cases.why: Traditional and Simplified differ for the eastern octants (東 vs 东) and agree for the others.

bearingOctant.doc: Which of the 8 compass points a bearing snaps to, 0–7 clockwise from North. One rule with two consumers that must agree: formatBearing turns it into a word, and every renderer`s compass needle turns it into a rotation. apps/mobile had a second, subtly different copy inside BearingArrow.tsx (no range normalisation); porting the screen to a second renderer would have made a third.

cases.name: belair-northeast-kerb-snaps-to-northeast
cases.why: Real: the northeast Belair place carries bearingDeg 54, which is why its label reads "Northeast-bound".

cases.name: belair-southwest-kerb-snaps-to-southwest
cases.why: The opposite kerb of the same landmark, bearingDeg 225 — the pair ADR-042 exists to keep apart.

cases.name: halfway-rounds-up
cases.why: Math.round rounds .5 away from zero, so 22.5 goes to Northeast rather than North. Pinned because a port using banker`s rounding would differ here and nowhere else.

cases.name: three-hundred-and-thirty-eight-wraps-to-north
cases.why: THE WRAP ROW. 337.5–360 rounds up to octant 8, which does not exist; the % 8 brings it back to North. A port that omitted it would index past the end of its label array.

cases.name: a-negative-bearing-normalises
cases.why: THE ROW THE OLD COMPONENT COPY WOULD HAVE FAILED. Its Math.round(deg / 45) * 45 has no range normalisation, so -100 gave it -90 — a needle pointing east while the label said west.

cases.name: a-bearing-past-a-full-turn-normalises
cases.why: The same gap from the other side: 415 is 55.
